<reason>Both sides argued at a high level and handled the pressure rounds honestly (PRO conceded "nothing" on issuer-less assets; CON conceded its regime removes no protection). The decisive question became whether CON's bespoke regime is the motion's alternative. CON's best material was genuinely strong: the securities charter's distinctive machinery (issuer registration, classification gatekeeping, an asset-gated SIPC backstop) does not fit the commodity core, and the solvent FTX affiliate was commodity-regulated, not a broker-dealer — showing the protections are portable. PRO, however, made the debate easier to decide for a third-party reader: the motion contrasts broker-dealer rules with a "distinct, lightly supervised" category, and CON admitted its regime is "not light by any honest definition." PRO answered the classification challenge with a workable test and the symmetric point that CON's venue faces the same sorting problem, handled Bitcoin/Ether via a commodities affiliate, and listed concrete venue-level broker-dealer duties (best execution, house-desk ban, surveillance) CON had never named. PRO slightly elided that the FTX affiliate was CFTC- rather than securities-regulated, and CON's clipped turn was a minor cost. Net: PRO's function-over-label framing and turning of CON's own concessions carried a clear but competitive win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Rebuttal 2 [B4.5]-[B4.6] and closing [B5.1]-[B5.2]: quoting CON's own admission that its regime is "not light by any honest definition" and recasting CON's FTX affiliate example as the motion run as a live experiment — the supervised intermediary survived, the "distinct" venue collapsed — reframed CON's strongest evidence as support for PRO.</best_rebuttal>
